summary: C.R.I.S is a 3D route planner that helps mission teams find safe walking routes for astronauts on Mars. We built a browser-based app that shows the terrain of a 10 × 10 km area of Jezero crater, around the Octavia E. Butler landing site, using open NASA data. As the user zooms in, the app loads 1 km HiRISE detail tiles. Users plan a route, and the app checks it against NASA slope and step-height limits. This responds to the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge by turning raw orbital data into a practical planning tool. It matters because crews will need safe surface routes on Mars, and checking a route before a crew walks it can help reduce risk.
details:
PROJECT DETAILS CREATED BY C.R.I.S.

1. INTRODUCTION

1.1 WHAT IS C.R.I.S?

C.R.I.S is a 3D route planner for astronauts on Mars. It lets users explore a 10 × 10 km area of Jezero crater, centered on the Octavia E. Butler landing site, and checks each walking route against NASA safety limits for slope and step height. The name stands for the tool’s purpose of helping crews plan routes safely across the surface.

1.2 WHO IS IT FOR?

It is aimed at mission planners, students, and anyone interested in Mars exploration. Students can explore the terrain and the hazard layers, and professionals can test routes against the safety limits and compare alternatives.

1.3 INSPIRATIONS

C.R.I.S was inspired by map tools such as Google Earth and Google Maps, which let users drag across a map, zoom from a distant view to close detail, and tilt the view. We applied that same way of exploring to Mars. The Map mode uses drag with inertia, cursor zoom, and tilt, so users can explore Jezero crater the way they would explore a city online. We were also inspired by NASA’s Perseverance mission and its public Mars data, which let us build the tool on real terrain instead of an invented map.

2. HOW IT WORKS

2.1 GEOSPATIAL DATA PIPELINE

A multi-stage Python pipeline processes a 10 × 10 km region of Jezero crater into a 1000 × 1000 grid with 10 m cells, plus 100 streamed tiles of 1 × 1 km. From the 1 m/px HiRISE digital terrain model, it computes elevation, slope (90th percentile), roughness at a 2 m scale, and a sky-view factor, which is used as a proxy for solar and radiation exposure. The pipeline also combines grayscale HiRISE orthomosaics at zoom levels 16 and 17 with the color from the Mars 2020 basemap to produce full-color terrain textures. It adds official geologic units, rock and talus cover, and THEMIS thermal amplitude.

2.2 ML HAZARD CLASSIFICATION

The autolabel stage creates training labels for 48 m terrain patches, using NASA safety rules and published geologic maps. Of 43,264 patches, 21,122 were labeled. A scikit-learn MLP classifier predicts safe, rough, and impassable zones, with 93.1% accuracy on 20 held-out 1 × 1 km tiles.

2.3 3D ENGINE AND TERRAIN STREAMING

The 3D engine is written in Rust with Bevy 0.20.1 and compiled to WebAssembly, rendering directly into an HTML canvas inside the web app. It uses three levels of detail. Distant chunks show a coarse 26 × 26 mesh with 40 m spacing. Chunks within 1,600 m stream a 251 × 251 detail mesh with 4 m spacing and 1024 px orthophotos. Chunks within 400 m load 2048 px zoom-17 orthophotos, about 0.5 m per pixel. Memory caps of 20 detail chunks and 4 high-resolution chunks keep browser memory use safe.

The user can move between three cameras: a Map mode with drag, zoom, and tilt; a Drone mode for free-flight inspection; and a Rover mode, which follows a 1:1 scale 3D model of the Perseverance rover.

2.4 PHYSICS-AWARE ROUTE PLANNER

The route planner runs A* search on the 10 m grid and does not cut corners past blocked cells. The slope limit adapts to the load the astronaut carries. The load factor is (body mass + suit mass + payload mass) × 3.71 divided by (body mass × 9.81), using defaults of 80 kg for the astronaut, 104 kg for the suit, and 20 kg for the payload. When this factor exceeds 1, NASA’s 20° Artemis EVA slope limit is scaled down.

Cells above the effective slope limit, with roughness above 0.30 m (the NASA suited step-height limit), or marked impassable are blocked. Traversable cells receive a weighted cost based on slope (weight 3), roughness (2), optical texture (1), rock cover (3), hazard (5), thermal amplitude (0.5), and sky-view exposure (0.5).

The planner also computes the shortest route allowed under the same limits and explains why the chosen route is safer, showing the reduction in rock exposure, the reduction in peak slope, and the extra distance.

2.5 WEB INTERFACE AND NASA DATA PROXY

The Next.js interface syncs with the simulation and provides layer toggles with legends, vertical exaggeration control, and an elevation and safety profile chart. Context panels show InSight weather, DONKI space weather, a MODIS Earth comparison, and a gallery of Perseverance raw images. All NASA data is served through server-side route handlers.

3. TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

  • Web and API: Next.js 16.4.6, React 19.3.0, TypeScript 5, Tailwind CSS 4.3.3, Vercel
  • 3D simulation and pathfinding: Rust 1.97.1, Bevy 0.20.1, pathfinding 4.16.0, wasm-bindgen 0.2.130
  • Data pipeline: Python with earthaccess, xarray, rioxarray, astropy, scikit-learn, geopandas, and numpy
  • Database and tooling: Supabase, pnpm 11.20.0

4. OBJECTIVES AND ACHIEVEMENTS

4.1 OBJECTIVE

Build a browser-based 3D Martian route planner for Jezero crater that uses real NASA data, streams high-resolution terrain, analyzes hazards in several layers, and checks routes against safety limits, all within 48 hours.

4.2 WHAT WE ACHIEVED

  • Built the Rust and Bevy terrain engine, compiled to WebAssembly, and running in a Next.js 16 web app.
  • Implemented three-level terrain streaming (40 m, 4 m, and about 0.5 m per pixel) across 100 km².
  • Built the Python pipeline, which produces eight or more data layers and a hazard classifier with 93.1% accuracy.
  • Tested the load-adjusted A* routing on 12 real point-to-point routes of at least 1.5 km. None had a safety violation, and roughness stayed between 0.10 and 0.24 m. Rock exposure dropped from 16% to 0% on one route and from 32% to 2% on another. Peak slope dropped from 19.5° to 5.5° on one route. The safe routes were 0 to 8% longer than the shortest allowed path.
  • Connected live and cached NASA data sources: DONKI space weather, Perseverance raw images, InSight weather, and MODIS land surface temperature.

5. LIMITATIONS

  • Imagery recency: The surface imagery comes from orbital mosaics and may not show recent small-scale changes.
  • Browser memory: Loading all 100 km² at full 0.5 m per pixel at once exceeds the memory of a modest browser, so the app streams by distance and caps the number of tiles.
  • Radiation and rock data: No public continuous radiation map or high-resolution rock-abundance map exists for Jezero yet. C.R.I.S uses the sky-view factor as an exposure proxy and the Stack et al. (2020) photogeologic units for rock cover.
  • Manual labels: The manual patch labels did not reach the 150-patch threshold during the hackathon, so the classifier trains on autolabel data based on NASA rules.
  • NASA endpoint: The api.nasa.gov Mars Rover Photos API was archived in October 2025, so Perseverance raw images are fetched directly from the mars.nasa.gov feed.

6. NEXT STEPS

  • Complete at least 150 manual hazard labels in the labels file, then retrain and compare the classifier against expert labels.
  • Validate the A* safety parameters against historical Perseverance drives.
  • Improve asset compression and caching so the full map runs smoothly on low-end laptops and tablets.
  • Extend the pipeline to more landing sites, such as Gale Crater, and add high-resolution THEMIS thermal data when it is published.

7. USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

The team used Claude (Anthropic), accessed through the omp coding agent, to help write the data pipeline, the Bevy simulation, the web bridge and API routes, the build script, and the user interface. The team defined the plan, the terrain features, and the safety logic. The hazard training labels were made by hand. Details are recorded in docs/SI_USAGE.md.

8. LINKS
